Yes, the story has an appropriate balance between scene and summary/exposition. 

The writer effectively uses compressed summary and exposition to span several months of the academic year (from autumn to March), provide essential background on the characters' class and family dynamics, and quickly bridge the gaps between major events (such as the nine days Lizzy stays away, or the progression of Mira's relationship with Johan). At the same time, the narrative slows down into vivid, real-time scenes—anchored by sharp, economical dialogue and specific physical details—for the crucial emotional turning points, such as Lizzy asking for money in the supermarket, the phone call confronting Mira about the report, and the quiet moments of tentative reconciliation. This alternation allows the story to cover a wide arc of character development at an engaging, well-modulated pace.
